title: How to Build a Daily Student Learning Tracker That Runs Itself
author: Phillip Alcock
summary: Phillip Alcock gives Year 9 science teachers a step-by-step workflow for automating daily accountability in a project-based learning classroom. Using Google NotebookLM connected to a Gemini Gem, the teacher uploads four prepared documents (the mission outline, a one-paragraph summary, a numbered assessment checklist and a daily I-can goals table) and the Gem generates a personalised tracking sheet for each student. He stresses that output quality depends on the source documents, includes a test run and verification checks, and suggests extensions such as differentiation layers and catch-up planning. The larger point is that students, not the teacher, carry the load of tracking where they stand against the goal.
points: The workflow replaces hand-written daily tracking notes with auto-generated student sheets built from the teacher's own mission outline.
The Gem is only as reliable as its four source documents, so the driving question, daily goals and assessment requirements must be separate and unambiguous.
Daily goals should be written in student-facing language describing what the student will do, not what the teacher will teach.
A Day 1 test run checked against the source documents catches invented content and an unlinked notebook before the full class rollout.
Shifting tracking to students changes the classroom question from whether they did the work to whether they can say where they are against the goal.
quotes: She was hand-writing notes after class, updating a shared spreadsheet, hoping students were checking it. It was working, sort of. But it was her carrying the cognitive load that her students should have been carrying themselves.
The driving question is the critical piece. “How can we help our community?” is too vague, the Gem will produce trackers that could apply to any subject and any year level.
As the photo explains: if any of those three elements is missing, vague, or incomplete, fix them now. You are building a machine. The machine is only as reliable as its source material.

The point of this step is machine-readability. When the Gem builds the self-assessment section of each tracking sheet, it pulls from this list. If two requirements are merged on one line, the Gem may treat them as one item and your students will never see the second.

Each goal should describe what a student will be able to do or understand by the end of that day, not what you plan to teach. The Gem prints this goal at the top of every tracking sheet it generates for that day, so the language needs to face the student, not the teacher.

If the Gem is inventing content producing questions or requirements that are not in your documents check that the notebook is still listed under Knowledge in the Gem settings. If it has become unlinked, re-attach it.

When students have a personalised tracker that names the day’s learning goal, ties the reflection prompts to that goal, and lists the assessment requirements they need to meet the question shifts. It is no longer “Did they do the work?” It becomes “Can they tell me where they are against the goal?
